analysis.one_liner: Sets due-process rights, counsel access, and oversight for people caught up in immigration arrests and detention.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: introduced by Senator Menendez with 3 cosponsors, it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in July 2009 and died there when the Congress ended in January 2011, with no vote ever held.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill responded to a problem its sponsors said was real: U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents being wrongly detained or deported by immigration enforcement after identity mix-ups. It would have required immigration officers to inform detainees of their rights in a language they understand, guaranteed access to a lawyer and a phone within hours, required charges within 48 hours and a judge's review within 72, barred immigration holds on anyone whose citizenship was not first verified, kept arrests away from schools, hospitals, churches, and courthouses, screened vulnerable people (children, pregnant women, caregivers, asylum seekers) for release instead of detention, and created an independent ombudsman to inspect detention facilities and handle complaints.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents wrongly caught in immigration sweeps, immigrants facing detention, and their families, who would gain counsel access, phone access, quick charges, verified immigration holds, protected locations, vulnerable-population release standards, and an independent complaint channel.

how_it_helps.text: Requires officers, before questioning a detainee, to advise them in their own language of the right to counsel, the right to remain silent, and that statements can be used against them; statements taken in violation cannot be used in removal proceedings.

Guarantees access to a lawyer at every stage of immigration enforcement, plus a list of free and low-cost legal services and free phone calls within 6 hours to a consulate, attorneys, courts, and oversight offices.

Requires a charging document within 48 hours of detention and a custody hearing before an immigration judge within 72 hours, and bars ICE from issuing a detainer unless an official confirms under oath that the person is not a U.S. citizen — aimed directly at mistaken detentions of citizens and lawful residents.

Prohibits arrests at schools, hospitals, places of worship, courthouses, funerals, and social service agencies, and requires screening within 72 hours so vulnerable people — children, pregnant women, sole caregivers, people over 65, asylum seekers, trafficking victims — are released unless detention is justified.

Creates an ICE Ombudsman inside DHS to conduct unannounced inspections of detention facilities, take confidential detainee complaints, investigate systemic problems, and report results to Congress annually.

Requires annual reports to Congress detailing who was swept up in worksite and fugitive operations — children, citizens, caregivers — and whether agents used force, entered homes without warrants, or coerced signatures.

analysis.who_pays: The Department of Homeland Security and its immigration enforcement agencies, which would bear new obligations: verified detainers, language access, 72-hour screenings, training, rulemaking, and a new oversight office, with costs funded by congressional appropriations; detention operators would hold fewer people as more detainees moved to supervised release programs.

drawbacks.text: The bill carries real costs for the enforcement system: mandatory verified alienage before any detainer, 72-hour custody hearings, and release standards for broad categories of detainees would slow operations and reduce the number of people ICE can hold pending removal proceedings.

The screening, training, rulemaking, secure-alternatives contracts, and new Ombudsman office are all funded by open-ended appropriations — 'such sums as may be necessary' — so taxpayers would foot an unquantified bill.

Broad protected-location rules barring arrests near schools, hospitals, churches, and other 'immediate vicinity' locations could give people seeking to avoid enforcement a map of safe zones, an objection enforcement officials would likely have raised.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections address a documented failure mode — citizens and lawful residents swept up by mistake — with due-process mechanics (verified holds, fast charges, counsel, judicial review) that are standard in criminal procedure, so the core is well-designed. The open-ended appropriation and some broad categorical rules would have drawn legitimate cost and enforcement-efficiency objections, but on balance the bill's benefits to people wrongly detained outweigh its administrative costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Menendez introduced the bill on July 30, 2009, joined by Senators Edward Kennedy and Kirsten Gillibrand.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.
The complete action history shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor consideration — before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Immigration enforcement as it then operated, and the detention system that filled beds with detainees, were left untouched because the bill never got a hearing. Citizens and lawful residents exposed to mistaken detention got no new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing detention and enforcement system

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, drafting protections against unlawful detention of citizens and residents.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no party split is visible; all four sponsors were Senate Democrats (3 of 56 Senate Democrats cosponsored) and there is no record of Republican support or opposition.

industries.industry: Private prison and immigration detention facility operators
industries.note: The bill would have moved vulnerable detainees out of custody into supervised 'secure alternatives' programs run by nonprofit contractors and required verified citizenship checks before detainers, shrinking the detained population. Fewer detainees means less revenue for facilities paid per detainee, including contractors.

industries.industry: Immigration legal services and nonprofit supervision providers
industries.note: The bill directs DHS to contract with nongovernmental organizations for screening, appearance assistance, and community supervision, and mandates distributing lists of free and low-cost legal services to detainees.

The bill imposes binding procedural limits on enforcement — verified detainers, 48-hour charges, 72-hour hearings, protected locations — while giving agencies new training mandates and an internal ombudsman structure that would add oversight and cost.
